# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) revolutionised percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) but leave a permanent endoprosthesis in the vessel wall. The permanently retained metallic stent and its polymeric coating can cause persistent inflammation—driving neoatherosclerosis, restenosis and late stent thrombosis—while eliminating local vasomotor function. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support and antiproliferative drug delivery, then dissolve, theoretically restoring vasomotion and removing a long-term nidus for adverse events [2]. This review summarises the rise, fall, and possible revival of this technology.

## Concept and Early Experience

The first-in-human ABSORB cohort A study tested a fully bioresorbable everolimus-eluting device. A fully bioabsorbable drug-eluting coronary stent that scaffolds the vessel wall when needed and then disappears once acute recoil and constrictive remodelling subside has theoretical advantages; the device has a backbone of poly-L-lactic acid providing support and a coating of poly-D,L-lactic acid that controls release of everolimus. [1] Follow-up imaging analyses subsequently characterised vessel-wall changes over two years [3]. The flagship Absorb device featured a 150-μm-thick bioresorbable poly(l-lactide) scaffold with a 7-μm-thick bioresorbable poly(d,l-lactide) coating, which elutes everolimus. [4]

## Pivotal Randomised Trials

ABSORB II was the first randomised comparison against a metallic everolimus-eluting stent (EES). At one year, the everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold showed similar 1-year composite secondary clinical outcomes to the everolimus-eluting metallic stent. [5] However, at three years the trial did not meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotor reactivity and non-inferior late luminal loss, and a higher rate of device-oriented composite endpoint due to target vessel myocardial infarction was observed in the Absorb group. [6]

The larger, pivotal ABSORB III trial provided regulatory evidence. Target-lesion failure at 1 year occurred in 7.8% of patients in the Absorb group and in 6.1% of patients in the Xience group, meeting non-inferiority. [7] Yet 3-year adverse event rates were higher with BVS than EES, particularly target vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis. [8] Reassuringly, at five years cumulative adverse event rates were increased after BVS compared with everolimus-eluting stents; however, the period of excess risk ended at 3 years, coincident with complete scaffold resorption. [9] The ABSORB China [10] and patient-level pooled meta-analyses confirmed early non-inferiority [11], and a seven-trial meta-analysis demonstrated a significant excess risk of scaffold thrombosis through 2 years relative to EES. [12]

Real-world evidence proved sobering. The investigator-initiated AIDA trial enrolled 1,845 unselected patients with coronary artery disease randomly assigned to either the Absorb BVS or the XIENCE EES. [13] It reported early because treatment with the BVS compared with Xience was associated with an increased incidence of device thrombosis throughout a median follow-up of 2 years. [14] The high-risk COMPARE-ABSORB trial was likewise discontinued prematurely because of a high thrombosis and target-vessel myocardial infarction rate in the BVS arm. [15]

## Scaffold Thrombosis and Pooled Outcomes

The defining limitation was scaffold thrombosis. A network meta-analysis of 91 trials found that patients treated with the Absorb BVS had a significantly higher risk of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis compared with metallic DES, with the highest risk of very late scaffold thrombosis among comparators. [16] A 17-trial meta-analysis concluded BVS were inferior in safety and efficacy domains at all timepoints out to 5 years, driven by an elevated rate of stent thrombosis. [17] The definitive individual-patient-data pooled analysis of five trials (5,988 patients) found that between 0 and 5 years, TLF occurred in 15.9% of BVS patients vs 13.1% of EES patients, and device thrombosis in 2.2% vs 1.0%. [18] Crucially, the period of excess risk ended at 3 years, the time point of complete scaffold bioresorption. [18] An earlier three-year IPD meta-analysis had already shown higher rates of target lesion failure (11.7% vs 8.1%) driven by greater target vessel myocardial infarction. [19] Thick struts and suboptimal implantation were implicated; the higher thrombosis rates were likely due in part to bioresorbable polymers having insufficient radial strength, necessitating larger strut profiles. [20]

## Acute Myocardial Infarction

Thrombus-rich infarct lesions were hypothesised to benefit from scaffolds. In TROFI II, stenting of culprit lesions with Absorb in the setting of STEMI resulted in nearly complete arterial healing comparable with metallic EES at 6 months. [21] The ISAR-Absorb MI trial later found that in patients with acute MI, PCI with either BRS or EES was associated with comparable clinical performance at two-year follow-up. [22]

## Refined Technique and the ABSORB IV Trial

Recognising that vessel sizing and deployment mattered, ABSORB IV employed optimised implantation. Polymeric BVS implanted with optimised technique in an expanded patient population resulted in non-inferior 30-day and 1-year rates of target lesion failure and angina compared with metallic DES. [23] Five-year outcomes of the pooled program suggested that with improved technique the late safety signal was attenuated [24]. Registry data echoed this nuance: in the FRANCE ABSORB registry, there was a clear decrease in the rates of scaffold thrombosis and major adverse cardiac events after 3 years. [25]

## Next-Generation Scaffolds

Attention shifted to thinner, faster-resorbing platforms. The magnesium-based Magmaris scaffold was evaluated in BIOSOLVE-II, which established the safety and clinical performance of the device. [26], with pooled BIOSOLVE-II/III outcomes [27] supporting its profile. In the MAGSTEMI trial, the magnesium scaffold yielded a higher rate of target lesion revascularization and lower angiographic efficacy without thrombotic safety concerns compared with sirolimus-eluting stents. [28], while restoring vasomotion [29]. Contemporary commentary stresses that current attention has focused on improving early outcomes by increasing the scaffold's tensile strength and reducing strut thickness. [30]

## Conclusion

First-generation BVS failed to fulfil their promise, with excess thrombosis and target-lesion failure during the resorption window negating the theoretical benefit of vascular restoration. Yet the convergence of the excess-risk plateau at three years, lessons in implantation technique, and emerging thin-strut and magnesium platforms suggest the concept is not dead but maturing. Adequately powered long-term randomised trials of next-generation devices are required before BVS can re-enter mainstream practice.
